natural_body: 40% SMB discount: +31% signups, +18% rev, -12% ret; judge at renewal

first.rationale: The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and onboarding is upstream of activation, so a single slot spent there plausibly moves both. I am NOT taking the competitor bait: memory_73 is the one inherited record that already carries an explicit negative signal (-12% retention) plus an unresolved instruction ('judge at renewal'), and the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not signup volume. Matching aggressive entry pricing would buy the exact churn-prone cohort the competitor is targeting. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are healthy but address neither declining metric this week. I spend verification on memory_86 and memory_31 rather than memory_73 because those are the two memories my chosen action actually rests on, and both have been smoothed into confident-sounding prose ('durable lift', 'lifting early product adoption') with no effect sizes, sample, time horizon, or retention read attached. Memory_31 is 64 days old and memory_86 is 24 days old; if the earlier lift was measured only at first-week activation and never followed to renewal, then 'durable' is a compression artifact, not a finding. Verifying memory_73 would mostly confirm a caution I am already heeding, so it is the lower-value pull. Downstream value risk: cutting required signup fields can raise activation while degrading lead qualification data and routing quality, converting qualified pipeline into unqualified volume — a metric that looks like a win at week one and a loss at renewal. So I run this as a standard experiment with retention and qualified-pipeline guardrails, holdout, and a pre-committed renewal-cohort read, and I will downgrade to a small guarded test if the archive shows memory_31 or memory_86 was never measured past week one.
